paras: The Daytona peninsula manhunt was a search by officers and a crowd of white citizens for an unnamed Black cyclist near Daytona, Florida, on 26 April 1903, during which open threats of lynching were made. The man was never found, and a suspect was released; the Daytona Gazette-News said the incident "came near precipitating mob violence."
According to the Gazette-News, Daytona was in "a feverish state of excitement" that spring after several crimes against white women attributed to Black men, one of whom was then in jail.

Miss Branch, daughter of E. A. Branch of Goodall, was walking on a lonely peninsula road when a Black man on a bicycle stopped a few yards from her, dismounted and waited. When he called to her to "come on," she fled screaming to the nearest house, and he rode off. The editor conceded that why he stopped "is known only to himself" but called his conduct "well calculated to alarm her."

Sheriff Turner, City Marshal Zuber and "a large number of citizens" then crossed the South bridge on a man hunt. The officers tried to calm the crowd, the editorial said, yet "open threats of lynching were heard" as it spread through the woods. Bridges were watched but the cyclist was not found, and a man arrested and taken before Miss Branch was released when she said he was the wrong man.

Rumors meanwhile spread that other women had been robbed and that a Black man had thrown a woman into the Halifax river, which the editor called "groundless lies." Had the cyclist been caught that evening, he wrote, "all the sheriffs and marshals on the East Coast could not have saved his neck."

The episode is known only from a Gazette-News editorial of 2 May 1903 headed "The Reign of the Liar," subtitled "He Is Injuring the Town and Inciting to Mob Violence." It blamed "sensation mongers and calamity liars" for the danger of a lynching, while presenting the earlier crimes as facts and the cyclist's behavior as alarming. No wire report, other white paper or Black-press account was found.

reader.title: Daytona peninsula manhunt and lynching threats (1903)
bases: A2 describes a manhunt by the sheriff, the city marshal and a large crowd of citizens for a Black cyclist during which 'open threats of lynching were heard'; the man was not found and no one was harmed, so this is a threatened lynching only.

A2 reports that the man was never found and that a suspect was released, so no one was killed; the crowd that threatened lynching numbered well over three and acted on an alleged offense against a white woman, but the threat was not carried out.
The only report is a single editorial in the local weekly A2; no news report, wire story or Black-press account was found.

accounts.label: Local editorial (Daytona Gazette-News)
accounts.gist: A Black cyclist frightened Miss Branch by stopping and calling to her; officers and a large crowd hunted him, lynching threats were heard, he was not found, and false rumors nearly turned the excitement into mob violence.

framing.detail: Under the headline 'The Reign of the Liar: He Is Injuring the Town and Inciting to Mob Violence', the editor condemned rumor-mongers for nearly causing a lynching but called the cyclist's conduct alarming, referred to an earlier accused man as 'a black brute', and said that if caught that evening the man could not have been saved.

sources.note: Editorial 'The Reign of the Liar': the only account of the Sunday incident on the peninsula, the manhunt, the lynching threats and the release of a suspect.
quotes: A case in point occurred last Sunday afternoon, and came near precipitating mob violence over on the peninsula.
